What does it mean to be optimistic? We think of optimism as an expectation that things will work out for the best. While we might accept that such expectations have motivational value - making it easier to deal with the struggle and strife we see in the world - we might still feel dubious about it from an intellectual perspective. Optimism is, after all, by its nature delusional; ‘realism’ or outright pessimism might seem more justifiable given the troubles of the present and the uncertainties of the future.

Those of us familiar with Voltaire’s celebrated novel Candide might be reminded of his character Dr Pangloss, and his refrain that all must be for the best ‘in this best of all possible worlds’. As Pangloss and his company are subjected to disaster, war, mutilation, cruelty and disease, his article of faith seems increasingly blind. Pangloss, a professor of ‘metaphysico-theologico-cosmolo-nigology’, is a vicious caricature of the great German polymath Gottfried Wilhelm Leibniz, and his catchphrase is Voltaire’s snappy formulation of the German’s attempt to provide a logical argument for optimism. Or, really, a theological argument. Leibniz didn’t set out to explain why some people are perpetually cheerful about their prospects, but why an all-powerful, all-seeing and all-loving God allows evil to exist in the world. This ‘problem of evil’ has been debated for millennia, but it was Leibniz who first attempted to reason his way to an answer... His inspiration came from his realisation... that the path taken by light through a system of prisms or mirrors always followed the ‘optimal’, path from source to destination. He soon realised that many other phenomena followed a similar ‘principle of optimality’ - including, perhaps, the entirety of God’s creation.

... Leibniz argued that God could have chosen from many laws and ingredients when making the world, but some combinations would not be internally consistent. So God, in His wisdom, chose the particular combination that led to a world that was both ‘simplest in hypotheses and richest in phenomena’. That might not be a perfect world... but it would be the best of all possible worlds. While there might be many possible ways to make a world, there’s only one optimal way. And this view of the world came to be known as optimism.

Leibniz’s view did not win instant acclaim. Critics sniffed at the idea... But it was Voltaire, almost half a century later, who dealt the killing blow. Candide proved enormously successful... Even today, many people are much more familiar with Voltaire’s satirical take than Leibniz’s rational one. But was Leibniz on to something?... The idea that there are many possible worlds is intuitively appealing in a time when ever fewer people accept the idea of a divine plan... Today, we think the responsibility lies with us.

That makes Leibnizian optimism more appealing than it has been for centuries... we cannot see or understand the whole design of the world... The key to making Leibniz’s version of optimism relevant... is to make ‘the best of all possible worlds’ an aspiration, not a statement of belief... The world, and the future, is always full of possibilities - and we can always strive to make it the best of all possible worlds.
passages.V2:
Platforms like Google, Facebook, and Amazon are not only shaping our economy, but our society—with questions of privacy, monopoly power, online racial discrimination, misinformation, hate speech, incitement, and impacts on mental health at the fore of the policy debate. In a democratic society, designing policies to mitigate such harms—while preserving platform benefits and staying true to widely held values—is difficult. It often involves balancing one person’s rights against another’s. Yet, across political lines, many Americans agree that Big Tech holds too much power. These monopolists squeeze consumers, workers, and small businesses, while their business model of engagement through outrage exacerbates societal polarization. A vigorous debate is underway over what new rules are needed for the digital age. However, Big Tech lobbyists have been trying to sidestep this democratic process by embedding restrictive digital rules into international trade agreements. Negotiated largely in secret, these rules would constrain efforts by governments to regulate privacy, data security, and market competition.

The goal is to construct a global digital framework where dominant platforms can operate with minimal oversight. These rules, if enacted, would prevent governments from adopting and enforcing policies meant to protect consumers and preserve competition. This approach echoes past trade negotiations used to protect corporate profits over the public interest. Just as Big Pharma used trade pacts to expand patent protections at the expense of affordable medicine, Big Tech is now pursuing trade-based constraints on digital governance. Some of the rules being pushed would label most competition policies as illegal trade barriers. This would tie the hands of governments attempting to curb platform dominance and protect smaller digital players. Other provisions would grant platforms and data brokers sweeping control over personal data, limiting countries’ ability to enforce privacy laws or restrict cross-border data flows for national security. Also at stake is the ability of governments to review algorithmic decision-making. These systems can determine access to loans, jobs, housing, and legal outcomes. Yet Big Tech is pushing rules that would prevent authorities from inspecting such algorithms, even to guard against discrimination or exploitation. Further provisions threaten consumer protections like “right to repair” laws, which help people update and fix their own devices affordably.

A key tactic of industry lobbyists has been to frame these issues as matters of foreign policy, claiming that Big Tech’s dominance is essential for national competitiveness. But conflating corporate profit with national interest obscures the truth: global leadership is better served by promoting rules that support both innovation and democratic oversight. Lobbyists also argue that secrecy protections are needed to shield innovation from foreign theft. Yet international trade rules already protect trade secrets. Blocking governments from inspecting AI or source code only ensures that firms in law-abiding countries escape accountability. While digital trade language may appear technical, the implications are clear. These proposals would effectively block governments from responding to public demands for greater accountability and regulation of digital platforms.

There is a genuine and necessary debate about how best to promote competition and prevent harm in the digital age. But such decisions should be made transparently, through open public discourse—not locked away in trade agreements that serve corporate interests over democratic values.

Then there’s “underconsumption core.” The new viral trend on Tik-Tok encourages consumers to be a little less spend-happy and more conscientious. It’s garnered plenty of attention off-platform, too: Google searches for “underconsumption core” have surged by 1150%. April Silva, a TikTok user and thrift store fan, defines it as a more minimal approach to shopping: You don’t need five winter coats when you have one perfectly good one. You don’t need every color of Stanley cup or “massive Shein hauls just for content,” she said. “Most of the clothing you see in people’s hauls are just trend pieces... What I choose to spend my hard-earned money on matters and I try to be smarter about it every day.”

Instead of pressing “buy now” on hyped products, underconsumption-core adherents lean into capsule wardrobes, using makeup until it’s “down to pan,” and shopping second-hand. In many ways, underconsumption core is the spiritual sister of deinfluencing, where influencers dissuade followers from buying cult-favorite products. Both fall into what might be called “recession-core influencing”: When money is tight and costs are rising, who can stomach buying a $42 highlighter?

Shelby Orme, a sustainable living influencer, thinks the trend is “100%” a response to our current economic situation. “I think it’s that and a response to the constant exposure to perfectly curated homes and wardrobes... The insidious introduction of TikTok Shop has added to the frustration.” Trends like these tend to be cyclical... Kosak, an instructor at Arizona State University, remembers a version of underconsumption core once called “minimalism.” “That was admittedly flawed... With trends like this, people sometimes swap one form of consumption for another.” Kosak isn’t surprised Gen Z is embracing a “consume only what you need” mindset. They’re constantly targeted by advertising, but each generation realizes they don’t need all of it.

Gen Z is also keenly aware of environmental issues tied to fast fashion... A Pew study shows that 76% of Gen Zers are worried about climate change, with 37% saying it’s their biggest concern. Jennifer Bertling, who runs a TikTok about her Chihuahua mix Milly, said her boomer parents practiced underconsumption core before it had a name. Now in Los Angeles, she takes satisfaction in giving things a second life... “There’s very little need to buy new.” She also limits food waste and reuses as much as possible. “It’s not aesthetic, but it’s hers,” she said of Milly’s original blanket in a video titled “Underconsumption Core: Dog Mom edition.” Christina Mychaskiw, co-host of the “Sustain This!” podcast, appreciates the trend, especially after her emotional spending led to debt... In a “no buy” year, she learned she was shopping for a fantasy version of herself.

As the trend has taken off, some users have turned it into a competition. “There’s a video of a woman sharing her sustainable life, and people were like, ‘Well, your fridge is full so you’re not underconsumption core.’” “We all have our version of how to be a better consumer,” Mychaskiw said. “It’s not about getting rid of everything...” Kosak agrees. Instead, she hopes the trend helps people gravitate toward purchases that are emotionally durable and meant to last. “It’s always better to step back and ask yourself: ‘What part of this is appealing to me, and why?’”
passages.V4:
Few tasks come as thankless as asking a scientific journal editor to correct a bad study. “I think that it [is] time to stop this never-ending story,” the editor of a diabetes journal said, refusing our request for data behind a study we deemed to have fatal statistical errors. As noted by Retraction Watch, the corresponding author said, "sharing data with a third party would breach participants’ consent and European data protection rules.” But such errors would invalidate preliminary positive results for a Web-based clinical decision support tool intended to help diabetes patients. Those are the people we were concerned about.

Unfortunately, such irresponsibility is all too common.

Science informs our medical care, flies us through the skies, and keeps us safe while driving. And yet, because it’s done by people, mistakes can be made. After all, to err is human. Scientific papers are riddled with errors; as many as 30 percent of cluster randomized controlled trials for childhood obesity may have been analyzed incorrectly. In psychology, 20 percent or more studies may have inconsistencies that cast doubt on their reliability. When mistakes happen, the costs can be high. Researchers say science is self-correcting, but often it isn’t or is unforgivably slow. For example, in the early 19th century, physicians misdiagnosed healthy infants with "enlarged" thymuses, mistakenly linking them to sudden infant death syndrome (SIDS). Radiation therapy was used on thousands of children, ultimately causing increased rates of thyroid and breast cancer and over 10,000 deaths. Although the error was recognized in the 1940s, a national campaign warning the public wasn't launched until 1977.

Serious errors occur in social sciences, too. Economists Carmen Reinhart and Kenneth Rogoff published influential research suggesting countries’ economic growth declines when debt exceeds 90 percent of GDP. Broadly cited by political leaders, this finding supported global austerity policies. Independent researchers later found significant calculation errors, omitting key data from five countries, reversing the findings to show growth increased, not declined. Reinhart and Rogoff acknowledged the error but argued against other criticisms and maintained their findings generally held. This case highlights common irresponsibility—authors failing to proactively disclose data and editors not requiring its availability. Had data been fully shared, errors might have been corrected sooner.

An egregious saga involved falsification in Alzheimer’s and Parkinson’s research by Eliezer Masliah, former director at the National Institute of Aging. Following a government investigation, Masliah was guilty of misconduct, leading to two retracted papers due to doctored images. An investigation reported 132 papers from 1997-2023 as suspect, significantly impacting therapeutic development. Many of us have seen loved ones suffer Alzheimer's debilitating losses. Tragically, current treatments offer limited relief. Despite researchers' efforts and millions spent, progress has been hindered by false leads.

Marc Tessier-Lavigne, a former Stanford president, resigned after several papers from his group contained manipulated images. Though exonerated personally, the review concluded he failed to decisively correct mistakes. This case highlights the dangers when senior scientists and journal editors don't uphold scientific integrity. Delays in correcting known errors harm public trust in science, stall progress, and endanger lives. Scientists and journals must unwaveringly commit to correcting errors; our collective welfare depends on it.

1.q:
The passage given below is followed by four alternate summaries. Choose the option that best captures the essence of the passage.

When something traumatic happens, whether it's a car accident or witnessing an act of violence, your brain starts working overtime to process and file the experience into memory. The brain is like a filing cabinet. Traumatic events are like massive piles of papers that overwhelm the system. This overload can lead to those memories being stored in a disorganized way, causing them to resurface as intrusive and distressing thoughts. However, recent research shows that if an individual plays Tetris after a traumatic event, the memories don't get imprinted on the brain as a traumatic experience. Playing a visually demanding game shortly after a traumatic experience engages the brain's visuospatial processing system—the same system responsible for storing visual memories of trauma. When you focus on fitting the shapes into neat rows, you effectively interrupt the intrusive memory formation associated with PTSD.
opts: Disorderliness in the brain causes trauma, but engaging in such tasks that occupy one’s memory can reduce PTSD symptoms.
Trauma overwhelms the brain’s memory system, but research suggests that playing Tetris after a traumatic event can prevent intrusive memories from forming.
Memories in the brain are affected by trauma, yet post-trauma activities that occupy visual processing prevent this.
Playing visually demanding games after trauma prevents PTSD by disrupting memory storage, which otherwise becomes disorganized and distressing.

21.q:
The passage given below is followed by four alternate summaries. Choose the option that best captures the essence of the passage.

Electro-agriculture replaces sunlight with electricity to support plant growth by converting CO₂ and water into metabolizable molecules. The process relies on electrolysis, which uses electric currents to induce chemical changes. Basic electrolysis doesn’t provide enough carbon for plants to bypass photosynthesis. To address this, a new study introduced a two-step process called tandem electrolysis. In the first step, CO2 is reduced to CO. In the second step, the CO is converted into acetate, a vital source of carbon for plants, providing them with energy and the building blocks needed for growth. Once the acetate is absorbed, plants convert it into key compounds, such as sugars and amino acids, that are essential for their metabolism, cell division and overall growth. This tandem process significantly boosts the efficiency of acetate production, making it a more viable nutrient source for plants.
opts: Tandem electrolysis enables the conversion of CO₂ into acetate, which plants use to grow, offering a more efficient process than traditional photosynthesis.
By replacing sunlight with electricity, electro-agriculture uses electrolysis to create acetate, which plants convert into essential compounds for growth.
Electro-agriculture uses electricity to support plant growth by generating acetate through tandem electrolysis, providing an efficient alternative to photosynthesis.
A new approach in electro-agriculture uses electrolysis to produce acetate from CO₂, improving plant metabolism and growth efficiency.

The source of the contradictions in the antidemocratic reaction is that it rests on an alliance between oppressors and many of their principal victims. It relies on the money of the few whose primary interest is to protect their power and privilege at the expense of the rest of society, and it relies on the votes of the many who will by and large suffer under the same extractive arrangements. To add to the mix, it trades in the ideas of an intellectual class that is parasitic on both sides—sucking money out of the oligarchs while offering right-wing identity politics and false hope to the resentful. The reliance on grievance and fear as a main political binding agent may offer the satisfaction of group identity, in the short term at least, but its contradictions are easily exposed.

Five jumbled-up sentences (labelled 1, 2, 3, 4, and 5), related to a topic, are given below. Four of them can be put together to form a coherent paragraph. Identify the odd sentence and key in the number of that sentence as your answer.

At its core, the abundance agenda overlooks the importance of public input in shaping infrastructure development.

More broadly, the abundance agenda reflects a deeper unwillingness to address the systemic flaws of modern capitalism.

Involving communities can lead to better land-use decisions and act as a democratic counterbalance to powerful corporate interests.

Zoning can separate industrial activities from residential areas and ensure that new homes are supported by adequate physical and social infrastructure.

Rather than eliminating tools like environmental review and zoning, these processes should be reformed through targeted improvements, such as strengthening state administrative capacity and encouraging growth in areas with strong public services.
